changedBeliefs: The pool-replacement-capacity estimand of the send-vs-sacrifice question is resolved AT THE PRODUCTION POOL SIZE (4 workers), and the answer overturns the concern that motivated exp 241/244: sacrifice does NOT deplete pool capacity — it is neutral-to-favorable. In an 8-request/4-worker barrier burst (fire 8 identical large sacrificing selects, 1-4 grab workers, 5-8 park, measure parked queue-wait = assignedAt-enqueuedAt via a decode-free ReaderPool.debugDispatchTimings hook, pool reset between bursts, 40x3 reps), the SEND (no-sacrifice) lane has the HIGHEST parked queue-wait — highest in all 3 reps, ~+500 us / +19% over the sacrifice lanes (send 3175 vs sacrifice-current 2652, sacrifice-eager 2684 us median). A large result's SendPort graph copy runs on the worker before it can take the next request and blocks the slot LONGER than Isolate.exit + an overlapped respawn. So at pool-4, sacrifice frees the slot sooner than not-sacrificing.

Eager respawn (start the post-sacrifice replacement spawn BEFORE the synchronous completion chain, instead of after) is REJECTED: sacrifice-eager (2684 us) equals sacrifice-current (2652 us) within ~1%, inside any pre-registered equivalence margin, on both queue-wait and makespan. The lifecycle asymmetry is real in code — the sacrifice branch completes a Completer.sync() (running the whole dispatch/emit/flush chain) before `unawaited(spawn(...))`, opposite of the non-sacrifice branch's `_notifyPool()`-before-complete — but at pool-4 the respawn overlaps other workers' in-flight queries and is off the parked request's critical path, so reordering it changes nothing observable. Not worth the reorder plus close/generation-safety surface.

Methodology confirmed: dispatch queue-wait (assignedAt - enqueuedAt) is the clean, decode-free observable for pool-capacity questions, and a barrier burst with the pool RESET between bursts (fresh-lifecycle treatment unit) avoids exp 241's state-changing-treatment confound. The immediate (unparked) requests measure ~0 queue-wait, confirming the barrier. This instrument (`ReaderPool.debugDispatchTimings`, null in production) is kept as reusable pool-measurement infrastructure.
nextSignals: Experiment A of the split is still open and is now the priority: a prepared-result, process-isolated handoff harness for the INTRINSIC transfer estimand (real ResultSet built before a Go-barrier; one fresh AOT process per observation; measure Go-sent-on-main -> raw result-handler-entered-on-main; ABBA-matched send vs Isolate.exit; record receive time as the FIRST op in the handler since the completer is synchronous). That isolates send-vs-exit transfer without pool or decode confounds. Experiment B (this run) has already removed the pool-capacity argument, so if Experiment A shows the intrinsic transfer is also a wash for typical shapes, the middle is a declared equivalence and the policy stays.

The pool-4 result dilutes the raw per-sacrifice respawn gap (parked requests wait on a busy worker's ms-scale query regardless of lane). `Database.open` clamps readerCount to a minimum of 2, so the peer's pool-size-1 diagnostic ceiling is not reachable through the public API; a benchmark-only pool-size override (or a direct ReaderPool.spawn(handle, 1) harness) would be needed to expose the raw gap. Low priority — pool-4 is the production regime and the direction there (sacrifice favorable) is unambiguous.

Standalone win independent of the transfer question, carried over from exp 241 and untouched here: the TEXT/shared-leaf misroute (sacrifice firing on a byte threshold for shared-string results that send ~2.9x cheaper). A routing guard keeping shared-leaf-dominated results on send is shippable now.

Eager respawn (and by extension the sacrifice reply-handler lifecycle) is closed unless the completion chain gets materially heavier (e.g. a future change that does more synchronous work inside `entry.emit`/`_flushQueue`), which would re-open the question of whether replacement launch should precede caller completion. Re-run this exact burst harness to check.

claims.text: Sacrifice opens no pool-capacity hole at the production pool size: the no-sacrifice lane had the highest parked queue-wait (~+19%), because send's copy blocks the worker longer than Isolate.exit plus an overlapped respawn. Eager respawn measured inert.
